text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Two soldiers were shot at the palace in Stockholm on Sunday when a fellow solider opened fire. Both needed hospital treatment. Police said the soldier had been arrested and neither of the two injured men -- an army captain and a national service soldier -- were seriously injured.

- Forestry consultant Jaakko Poyry of the world's biggest forestry consultancy group, Poyry COnsulting Group, says Sweden's forestry industry is too small to satisfy southeast Asian demand but that is the region where the industry will see the greatest growth. He says Nordic forestry companies must make moves to southeast Asia where 50 paper plants are under construction.
- Police are increasing protection for women who are threatened or attacked through a range of projects. Some women are being given security alarms.

- The media director for the Modern Times Group (MTG), Pelle Tornberg, a former journalist, wants to list the company on the Stockholm bourse, he says in an interview with the newspaper. MTG interests include television stations TV3, TV6, ZTV and free newspaper Metro. It is part of the Kinnevik media group that releases its 1996 results next month.

- Swedish telecoms group Ericsson warns about overheating of Information Technology (IT) companies on the Stockholm bourse after a spectacular rise in the sector last year. Chief executive Lars Ramqvist says in an interview that the main chances for growth in these companies is overseas and not in Sweden.

- Ericsson's Ramqvist says the Internet will give his company a new market and he is very optimistic that volumes will increase. However before the profits start to come in he said telephone operators and media companies must decide which techology they are going to invest in.

- Local changes are continuing to create problems for Sweden's largest commercial television station, TV4. The newspaper says the station could face new opposition from the state over recent negotiations designed for expansion.
